content.content: Exit code 2 # T3 Code T3 Code is a minimal GUI for coding agents. A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients. You can think of T3 Code as an open source "bring-your-own-subscription" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor. ## What makes T3 Code special? We have over 500,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on. ### 1. Open at the core T3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way. ### 2. Performance without compromise Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact. ### 3. Remote ready The architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported. ### 4. Multi-surface T3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**. **Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing "app.t3.codes" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable. **Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app. **Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely. ## A note from Theo I like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising. Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion. The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here. Of note: Most T3 Code contributions will come from T3 Code itself, often controlled remotely. This means you should be careful about accessing data, killing dev servers, and other things that may damage the T3 Code instance that the contributor is using. ## A small glossary We need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language: - **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code. - **we, us, and maintainers** mean Theo, Julius and the people building T3 Code. These are who you are talking to now. - **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents. - **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you. - **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode. - **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI. - **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns. - **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory. - **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project. - **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing. - **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory. ## The three ways to hurt yourself 1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc//cwd` is your worktree. 2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. 71	- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is "not supported here".
72	- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.
73	- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.
74	- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.
75	- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.
76	- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.
77	
78	## Dev servers
79	
80	- `vp i` installs. Worktrees get this from the t3.json setup script; if module resolution looks broken, it probably did not run.
81	- Setup runs in the background. While `.t3/setup-running` names a live PID, wait for it and do not run `vp i`. It ends with `.t3/setup-done` or `.t3/setup-failed` (with the error tail). With no marker at all, setup never ran here, so run `vp i` yourself.
82	- `vp run dev` starts server and web. In a worktree, state defaults to that worktree's gitignored `.t3`, which deliberately outranks an ambient `T3CODE_HOME` so you cannot land on shared state by accident. An explicit `--home-dir` still wins.
83	- Ports derive from the worktree path and are stable across restarts, but read the real ones from the `[dev-runner]` line since occupied ports shift.
84	- Sharing over the tailnet is three steps: run `vp run dev --share` in the background, wait for the `pairingUrl:` line in its output, then give that full URL to an unpaired browser. Do not wire up `tailscale serve` by hand, open the URL yourself, or consume the user's pairing link. A browser with the reusable dev cookie can use the bare origin. If a normal one-time token was consumed, mint a fresh one with `node apps/server/src/bin.ts pair`. 85	- To reuse web dev auth across worktrees, configure one fixed `T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN` in the main checkout's gitignored `.env`. The `t3.json` setup links that file into worktrees. Never commit or publish the token or a startup URL. See [Reusable dev credential](docs/operations/development.md#reusable-dev-credential).
86	- Stop what you started, by the PID you tracked. See rule 1.
87	- Need a second checkout? `git worktree add` it next to this worktree, not in `/tmp`. Remove it when done.
88	
89	## Test data
90	
91	An empty database is a bad test. Seed your worktree's `.t3` with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state:
92	
93	- The first `vp run dev` in a worktree does this for you when its database is missing and the source is at most 500 MiB. Larger sources warn and dev starts with an empty database. `--no-seed` or `T3CODE_DEV_SEED=0` skips seeding. Manual migration still accepts larger sources and may use substantial disk space before pruning.
94	- Run `vp run migrate-dev-db` with your dev server stopped to refresh. It rebuilds `<worktree>/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite` from a read-only snapshot of `~/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite`, the developer's real data. It keeps recent projects and their stopped threads, and drops scheduled tasks, pending work, and auth sessions, so your dev server never runs the developer's agents. Raise `--projects` and `--threads-per-project` for more data.
95	- Refresh `statev2.sqlite`, not `state.sqlite`. The server copies the V1 `state.sqlite` only when `statev2.sqlite` is missing.
96	- Bring `secrets` and `settings.json` only if the flow under test needs them.
97	- Copy in, never symlink. Data flows one way: into your sandbox, never back out.
98	
99	## Verifying
100	
101	- Before you push, run `vp run check:changed`. It runs CI's fast checks for changed files: format, lint, knip, typecheck of affected packages and dependents, and tests beside changes. CI still runs the full test suites.
102	- While you iterate, run `vp test run <files>`. For big files, add `-t "<name>"`.
103	- Use `vp run typecheck`, not `npx tsc`; it caches per package. Both run tsc-rs (`typescript` is the `@tsc-rs/typescript` drop-in).
104	- Run `node -e` snippets from `apps/server` or the owning package. `effect` does not resolve from the repo root.
105	- Test behavior that can break, such as orchestration and event-sourcing, provider protocol translation, auth and permission guards, persistence and migrations, external-format parsing, race fixes, and the logic a bug fix changed. Leave out tests for what types already guarantee, trivial logic, copy text, smoke runs, mock-call mirrors, callback wiring, and props rendered to static markup.
106	- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits.
107	- Test at one layer: the lowest one that fails on `main`. Do not repeat the case in a wrapper test, at each call site, or in web and mobile copies of the same logic.
108	- [Testing](docs/internals/testing.md) carries these same test rules, plus review guidance, for review bots. Change both together.
109	- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No `vp check`, no `vp run -r test`, no `vp run -r typecheck` unless I ask. CI owns the full suite.
110	- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
111	- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason, in an existing case of the module's test file where one fits), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures as their proof and no test: do not add UI tests for nitpicks, and do not ask for one in review when a capture already shows it. A server-only fix with no visible surface ships the test plus a short runtime transcript.
112	- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong. Concretely:
113	  - `it.effect` runs on a `TestClock`; `Effect.sleep` only advances through `TestClock.adjust`. `it.live` is wall-clock and only for subprocess or network fixtures.
114	  - No `yieldNow` or `sleep` polling loops. Await the `Deferred`, take from the `Queue`, or drain the worker.
115	  - No per-test timeout argument or `retry`. The project timeout is the ceiling, and flaky tests are fixed, not retried.
116	  - No `performance.now()` or `Date.now()` deltas. Assert on events and counts, not elapsed time.
117	  - Browser tests assert through `expect.element` or `vi.waitFor`, never `requestAnimationFrame` or `transitionend`.
118	  - `vi.mock` factories must not spread a real module that pulls in Shiki or the diff workers.
119	  - `it.skip` and friends need a tracking issue on the line above: `// quarantine: #1234 <why>`.
120	  - Lint enforces this: `t3code/no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip`, `t3code/no-frame-waits-in-browser-tests`, `t3code/no-wall-clock-in-tests`, `t3code/no-real-time-wait-in-tests`, `t3code/no-polling-loop-in-tests`.
121	- Web browser tests are `*.browser.test.tsx` or `*.browser.test.ts` and render with `await using screen = await render(...)` from `apps/web/test/render.tsx`. `t3code/require-disposable-render` errors on the old patterns.
122	  - Acquire what the test drives after mounting (fake timers it advances, spies it sets up after mounting) after the render, so it disposes before the unmount. Anything the first render reads comes before it.
123	  - A helper that renders and then waits or clicks puts the screen in an `AsyncDisposableStack` and `move()`s it out only on success, so a failed wait still unmounts.
124	  - `rerender` needs a fresh element on every call.
125	  - No lifecycle hooks and no module-level mutable state. Shared mock state that `vi.mock` factories read is reset by a `setup()` call at the top of the test.
126	  - `router` is on by default. Pass `router: false` only with a one-line comment saying why.
127	
128	  ```tsx
129	  it("saves on Enter", async () => {
130	    const onSave = vi.fn();
131	    using _now = vi.spyOn(Date, "now").mockReturnValue(0);
132	    await using screen = await render(<TitleEditor onSave={onSave} />, { router: "/threads/1" });
133	    await userEvent.type(screen.getByRole("textbox"), "Title{Enter}");
134	    expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Title");
135	  });
136	  ```
137	
138	- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.
139	
140	- Real agent turns cost money. To watch a turn stream through the pipeline and UI, use the free `Replay (dev)` provider that `vp run dev` registers; [test-t3-app](.agents/skills/test-t3-app/SKILL.md) shows how to start one. Use a real provider only when the change depends on that provider's behavior, and then pick its cheapest model, such as Haiku for Claude or Luna for Codex.
141	
142	For authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is an install step, not a blocker. Run `vp run mobile:install <ios|android> [device-id]` on the device host before starting Metro; it targets the only booted simulator or connected Android device when the id is omitted. It installs the dev client for this checkout's native fingerprint from the shared cache in seconds and builds only when no machine has built it yet, so prefer it over `expo run:*`, `xcodebuild`, or `gradlew`, which rebuild from scratch. Its stdout is one JSON line; build output goes to the log it names. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.
143	
144	## Evals
145	
146	`evals/` checks how real models behave with T3 Code's model-facing text: agent instructions, MCP tool descriptions and schemas, and generated titles. Before you change that text, read [evals/README.md](evals/README.md) and run the evals it names. When you fix a model behavior bug, add a case that fails before the fix.
147	
148	## Pull requests
149	
150	- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
151	- If `origin` is git.cafe, follow [GitCafe mirror](docs/operations/development.md#gitcafe-mirror-optional): push to `origin`, open and track PRs with `cafe` and their git.cafe URLs, and keep `gh` for merging.
152	- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.
153	- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
154	- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
155	- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
156	- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.
157	- When babysitting: call `watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you on checks, comments, or conflicts. Do not poll or sleep. Verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.
158	
159	## Documentation
160	
161	Most code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.
162	
163	- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
164	- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
165	- A local reason the code can't show goes in a short nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
166	- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
167	- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
168	- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.
169	- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.
170	
171	## Plans and work artifacts
172	
173	- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
174	- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.
175	- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.
176	
177	## How it works
178	
179	Clients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.
180	
181	Architecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`
182	
183	## Where code lives
184	
185	- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.
186	- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.
187	- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.
188	- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.
189	- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.
190	- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency. If it is missing (sparse checkout), read a file with `git show origin/main:.repos/<path>`.
191	
192	## Taste
193	
194	- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Orchestration stays pure, UI stays dumb.
195	- Client mutations use `createEnvironmentRpcCommand`. Add protected methods to `CLIENT_GUARDED_RPC_SCOPES` in contracts and use the command's `permissionAtom` for UI availability. Grants are checked at execution against the destination environment; the server remains authoritative. Keep raw RPC clients inside `rpc/`, and extend the permission behavior tests when adding a protected method.
196	- Server features are services; transports stay thin. A `ws.ts` RPC handler, HTTP route, or MCP tool decodes input, calls one service method, and maps errors. See [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md).
197	- `apps/web/src/components/ui` exports own their look. Pick a `variant` or `size`; do not restyle one with `className`. If none fits and the look is a generic concept, add a variant to the component; a look that belongs to one feature stays in that feature's own component, not in `components/ui`. Layout classes (width, flex, margin, position) belong on the parent. `shadcn/no-restyle` fails lint on violations. See [Web UI](docs/internals/web-ui.md).
198	- Reusable Effect functions use `Effect.fn("Service.operation")` with a stable span name, not a
199	  function wrapping `Effect.gen`. Keep `Effect.gen` for inline programs and layer construction.
200	  Use `Effect.fnUntraced` only when spans would be too frequent (stream chunks, per-event
201	  projection, tight loops) or duplicate an existing tracing boundary; explain that choice nearby.
202	  Named `Effect.fn` creates a span; the unnamed form does not. Preserve existing span names and
203	  options, and pass combinators as additional function-builder arguments.
204	- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
205	- Default to no comment. Write one only for a constraint, an external quirk, or an invariant the code can't show, in one line where you can and four at most. Don't restate names or signatures, narrate steps, record history, or explain the fix you just made; the PR carries that. `t3code/no-low-value-comments` enforces the length cap and the mechanical cases.
206	- React effects are for synchronizing with something outside React. Derive in render and act in handlers instead of syncing state, but don't hide real lifecycle work in refs or stores to dodge one. The `t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync` lint rule reports every effect; one that stays states its reason with `// oxlint-disable-next-line t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync -- <why>`.
207	- Our users drive agents all day and notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations; they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
208	- If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so loudly and get a human sign-off before breaking it.
209	
210	## Additional tips
211	
212	- Don't verify with browsers or computer use unless the user explicitly agrees or requests it.
213	- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features.

- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code.

- **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents.
- **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you.
- **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode.
- **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI.
- **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns.
- **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory.
- **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project.
- **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing.
- **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory.

## The three ways to hurt yourself

1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc/<pid>/cwd` is your worktree.
2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. Reading it and copying from it are fine, and a good way to get real test data (see Test data). Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.
3. **Baking in origins.** Never set `VITE_HTTP_URL` or `VITE_WS_URL` for dev. Dev is single-origin and Vite proxies `/api`, `/ws`, `/oauth`, and `/.well-known`. Setting them bakes localhost into the bundle and silently breaks every remote browser.

  - `vi.mock` factories must not spread a real module that pulls in Shiki or the diff workers.
  - `it.skip` and friends need a tracking issue on the line above: `// quarantine: #1234 <why>`.
  - Lint enforces this: `t3code/no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip`, `t3code/no-frame-waits-in-browser-tests`, `t3code/no-wall-clock-in-tests`, `t3code/no-real-time-wait-in-tests`, `t3code/no-polling-loop-in-tests`.
- Web browser tests are `*.browser.test.tsx` or `*.browser.test.ts` and render with `await using screen = await render(...)` from `apps/web/test/render.tsx`. `t3code/require-disposable-render` errors on the old patterns.
  - Acquire what the test drives after mounting (fake timers it advances, spies it sets up after mounting) after the render, so it disposes before the unmount. Anything the first render reads comes before it.
  - A helper that renders and then waits or clicks puts the screen in an `AsyncDisposableStack` and `move()`s it out only on success, so a failed wait still unmounts.
  - `rerender` needs a fresh element on every call.
  - No lifecycle hooks and no module-level mutable state. Shared mock state that `vi.mock` factories read is reset by a `setup()` call at the top of the test.
  - `router` is on by default. Pass `router: false` only with a one-line comment saying why.

  ```tsx
  it("saves on Enter", async () => {
    const onSave = vi.fn();
    using _now = vi.spyOn(Date, "now").mockReturnValue(0);
    await using screen = await render(<TitleEditor onSave={onSave} />, { router: "/threads/1" });
    await userEvent.type(screen.getByRole("textbox"), "Title{Enter}");
    expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Title");
  });
  ```

- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.

- Real agent turns cost money. To watch a turn stream through the pipeline and UI, use the free `Replay (dev)` provider that `vp run dev` registers; [test-t3-app](.agents/skills/test-t3-app/SKILL.md) shows how to start one. Use a real provider only when the change depends on that provider's behavior, and then pick its cheapest model, such as Haiku for Claude or Luna for Codex.

For authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is an install step, not a blocker. Run `vp run mobile:install <ios|android> [device-id]` on the device host before starting Metro; it targets the only booted simulator or connected Android device when the id is omitted. It installs the dev client for this checkout's native fingerprint from the shared cache in seconds and builds only when no machine has built it yet, so prefer it over `expo run:*`, `xcodebuild`, or `gradlew`, which rebuild from scratch. Its stdout is one JSON line; build output goes to the log it names. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.

## Evals

`evals/` checks how real models behave with T3 Code's model-facing text: agent instructions, MCP tool descriptions and schemas, and generated titles. Before you change that text, read [evals/README.md](evals/README.md) and run the evals it names. When you fix a model behavior bug, add a case that fails before the fix.

## Pull requests

- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
- If `origin` is git.cafe, follow [GitCafe mirror](docs/operations/development.md#gitcafe-mirror-optional): push to `origin`, open and track PRs with `cafe` and their git.cafe URLs, and keep `gh` for merging.
- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.
- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.
- When babysitting: call `watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you on checks, comments, or conflicts. Do not poll or sleep. Verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.

## Documentation

Most code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.

- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
- A local reason the code can't show goes in a short nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.
- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.

## Plans and work artifacts

- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.
- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.

## How it works

Clients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.

Architecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`

## Where code lives

- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.
- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.
- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.
- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.
- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.
- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency. If it is missing (sparse checkout), read a file with `git show origin/main:.repos/<path>`.

## Taste

- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Orchestration stays pure, UI stays dumb.
- Client mutations use `createEnvironmentRpcCommand`. Add protected methods to `CLIENT_GUARDED_RPC_SCOPES` in contracts and use the command's `permissionAtom` for UI availability. Grants are checked at execution against the destination environment; the server remains authoritative. Keep raw RPC clients inside `rpc/`, and extend the permission behavior tests when adding a protected method.
- Server features are services; transports stay thin. A `ws.ts` RPC handler, HTTP route, or MCP tool decodes input, calls one service method, and maps errors. See [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md).
- `apps/web/src/components/ui` exports own their look. Pick a `variant` or `size`; do not restyle one with `className`. If none fits and the look is a generic concept, add a variant to the component; a look that belongs to one feature stays in that feature's own component, not in `components/ui`. Layout classes (width, flex, margin, position) belong on the parent. `shadcn/no-restyle` fails lint on violations. See [Web UI](docs/internals/web-ui.md).
- Reusable Effect functions use `Effect.fn("Service.operation")` with a stable span name, not a
  function wrapping `Effect.gen`. Keep `Effect.gen` for inline programs and layer construction.
  Use `Effect.fnUntraced` only when spans would be too frequent (stream chunks, per-event
  projection, tight loops) or duplicate an existing tracing boundary; explain that choice nearby.
  Named `Effect.fn` creates a span; the unnamed form does not. Preserve existing span names and
  options, and pass combinators as additional function-builder arguments.
- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
- Default to no comment. Write one only for a constraint, an external quirk, or an invariant the code can't show, in one line where you can and four at most. Don't restate names or signatures, narrate steps, record history, or explain the fix you just made; the PR carries that. `t3code/no-low-value-comments` enforces the length cap and the mechanical cases.
- React effects are for synchronizing with something outside React. Derive in render and act in handlers instead of syncing state, but don't hide real lifecycle work in refs or stores to dodge one. The `t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync` lint rule reports every effect; one that stays states its reason with `// oxlint-disable-next-line t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync -- <why>`.
- Our users drive agents all day and notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations; they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
- If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so loudly and get a human sign-off before breaking it.

## Additional tips

- Don't verify with browsers or computer use unless the user explicitly agrees or requests it.
- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features.

name: Agent Context Budget

# Fails when a PR raises a value in agentContextBudget.json above main's. AgentContextBudget.test.ts
# keeps that file equal to the measured context, so the context cannot grow by editing the file.
# To accept growth on purpose, a maintainer adds the agent-context-increase label.
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled, unlabeled]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: agent-context-budget-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  budget:
    name: Agent context budget
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 5
    env:
      BUDGET: apps/server/src/provider/agentContextBudget.json
      ALLOW_INCREASE: ${{ contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'agent-context-increase') }}
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          sparse-checkout: apps/server/src/provider/agentContextBudget.json
          sparse-checkout-cone-mode: false

      - name: Compare with main
        run: |
          git fetch --quiet --depth=1 origin main
          if ! git cat-file -e "FETCH_HEAD:$BUDGET" 2>/dev/null; then
            echo "main has no agent context budget yet."
            exit 0
          fi
          git show "FETCH_HEAD:$BUDGET" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/main.json"
          grown=$(jq -r --slurpfile main "$RUNNER_TEMP/main.json" '
            to_entries[]
            | select($main[0][.key] != null and .value > $main[0][.key])
            | "\(.key): \($main[0][.key]) -> \(.value) (+\(.value - $main[0][.key]))"
          ' "$BUDGET")
          if [ -z "$grown" ]; then
            echo "Agent context is not larger than main."
            exit 0
          fi
          printf 'Agent context grew compared to main:\n%s\n' "$grown"
          if [ "$ALLOW_INCREASE" = "true" ]; then
            echo "Accepted by the agent-context-increase label."
            exit 0
          fi
          echo "::error file=$BUDGET::Agent context grew compared to main. Cut the added text, or ask a maintainer to add the agent-context-increase label."
          exit 1

content.content:
# Testing

Rules for writing tests, and for asking for them in review. AGENTS.md carries the same writing rules under Verifying; change both together.

## What to test

- Test behavior that can break, such as orchestration and event-sourcing, provider protocol translation, auth and permission guards, persistence and migrations, external-format parsing, race fixes, and the logic a bug fix changed. Leave out tests for what types already guarantee, trivial logic, copy text, smoke runs, mock-call mirrors, callback wiring, and props rendered to static markup.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits.
- Test at one layer: the lowest one that fails on `main`. Do not repeat the case in a wrapper test, at each call site, or in web and mobile copies of the same logic.
- In review, ask for a missing test only when it would catch a real regression. Do not ask for one assertion per constant, label, or `switch` case. Flag a new test that breaks the rules above, and name the fix: fold it into the existing case or table, delete it, or keep one layer.
- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason, in an existing case of the module's test file where one fits), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures as their proof and no test: do not add UI tests for nitpicks, and do not ask for one in review when a capture already shows it. A server-only fix with no visible surface ships the test plus a short runtime transcript.

## Waiting for work

- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong. Concretely:
  - `it.effect` runs on a `TestClock`; `Effect.sleep` only advances through `TestClock.adjust`. `it.live` is wall-clock and only for subprocess or network fixtures.
  - No `yieldNow` or `sleep` polling loops. Await the `Deferred`, take from the `Queue`, or drain the worker.
  - No per-test timeout argument or `retry`. The project timeout is the ceiling, and flaky tests are fixed, not retried.
  - No `performance.now()` or `Date.now()` deltas. Assert on events and counts, not elapsed time.
  - Browser tests assert through `expect.element` or `vi.waitFor`, never `requestAnimationFrame` or `transitionend`.
  - `vi.mock` factories must not spread a real module that pulls in Shiki or the diff workers.
  - `it.skip` and friends need a tracking issue on the line above: `// quarantine: #1234 <why>`.
  - Lint enforces this: `t3code/no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip`, `t3code/no-frame-waits-in-browser-tests`, `t3code/no-wall-clock-in-tests`, `t3code/no-real-time-wait-in-tests`, `t3code/no-polling-loop-in-tests`.

## Web browser tests

- Web browser tests are `*.browser.test.tsx` or `*.browser.test.ts` and render with `await using screen = await render(...)` from `apps/web/test/render.tsx`. `t3code/require-disposable-render` errors on the old patterns.
  - Acquire what the test drives after mounting (fake timers it advances, spies it sets up after mounting) after the render, so it disposes before the unmount. Anything the first render reads comes before it.
  - A helper that renders and then waits or clicks puts the screen in an `AsyncDisposableStack` and `move()`s it out only on success, so a failed wait still unmounts.
  - `rerender` needs a fresh element on every call.
  - No lifecycle hooks and no module-level mutable state. Shared mock state that `vi.mock` factories read is reset by a `setup()` call at the top of the test.
  - `router` is on by default. Pass `router: false` only with a one-line comment saying why.

  ```tsx
  it("saves on Enter", async () => {
    const onSave = vi.fn();
    using _now = vi.spyOn(Date, "now").mockReturnValue(0);
    await using screen = await render(<TitleEditor onSave={onSave} />, { router: "/threads/1" });
    await userEvent.type(screen.getByRole("textbox"), "Title{Enter}");
    expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Title");
  });
  ```
=====
# Performance regression checks

The v2 transport has a focused regression command:

```bash
vp run test:perf:v2-wire
```

It exercises the real v2 projection and client reducers. This matters because the older
built-app benchmark fixtures seed v1 orchestration events; running those fixtures against a v2
client can produce reassuring timings while missing the active transport path.

The v2 checks pin these invariants:

- Cold opens and history pages stop at about 1 MiB of encoded rows. A window that holds a user
  turn also stops at 10 user turns (20 on older pages) or 500 rows, so ordinary turns stay whole.
  Any other window, including the inside of one turn longer than 500 rows, stops at 75 rows. The
  snapshot query applies the same rule before it decodes payloads. Clients can opt into deferring
  large work groups until expansion. Messages and items outside those groups remain in normal
  history paging. Required control records and
  the at-least-one-row rule can exceed the byte target; it is not a hard cap.
- The bounded snapshot does not retain the full duplicate conversation-message table.
- Older activity is fetched in bounded HTTP pages and merged without disturbing the live scroll
  window.
- Clients with confirmed history paging opt into socket snapshot fallbacks that use the same
  bounded recent-history window and carry the cursor needed to fetch older history. Older clients
  and WebSocket-only starts retain the compatible full-snapshot fallback.
- Snapshot queries bound timeline reads per fork ancestor, not total rows: dependency and
  control records still accompany the window. Smaller socket frames alone do not establish a
  whole-server memory reduction.
- Resume catch-up checks the original 1 MiB persisted-payload budget before decoding, then
  replays at most 128 thread events and 1 MiB of projected event JSON before falling back to a
  snapshot. Raw JSON bytes are not a heap-memory cap. Raising this budget merely because output
  projects small can increase server allocations on repeated large tool updates.
- Raw command output, dynamic-tool result bodies, and inline file-change bodies are omitted at
  the wire boundary, including small outputs. Explicit failure flags and bounded result IDs
  preserve status and grouped action counts without shipping those bodies. Reasoning text,
  command lines, and search results ship when their work group loads. Subagent prompts and results
  and checkpoint control records still accompany the initial window.
  Persisted events remain complete; the existing diff endpoints still provide file content when
  requested.
  Explicit cross-environment transcript exports preserve full tool bodies so the destination
  agent can read the context. The export rejects timeline JSON above the file attachment limit
  before sending it; the client still applies its attachment limit to the complete file.
- Live command output reaches a client only through `orchestration.subscribeCommandOutput`, which
  an expanded command row opens and closes with itself. Raw output deltas are never orchestration
  events: adapters send them to the
  [command output hub](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/CommandOutputHub.ts) ahead of
  ingestion, which keeps one bounded tail per running command and throttles each subscriber. Do not
  route output deltas through `turn_item.updated`: a busy command would flood the event store and
  block ingestion for every other thread.
- The initial shell contains active navigation rows only. Archived rows use the dedicated archive
  query, and transcript message bodies stay in thread detail regardless of message size.
- Shell resume sends deltas plus compact repository-enrichment metadata, not another full project
  and thread snapshot.
- Auto, steer, and restart sends resolve delivery from authoritative state inside the
  server's per-thread dispatch lock. Model selection and identified-checkpoint rollback also
  dispatch without first fetching a full thread projection when the server advertises support.
  Older servers retain projection-based validation. Explicit start sends already skipped that
  read, so this saving does not apply to every client send path.

When changing projection schemas, paging, shell synchronization, or thread state, run this command
alongside the focused package typechecks and a real-client pass on every affected surface. The
transport performance fixtures validate contract encoding and compare pre-compression RPC JSON
for the same synthetic workload, preserving historical application-object counts separately.
These are neither compressed WebSocket captures nor measurements of server RSS, and command
fixtures exclude unrelated settings calls and subscription events. Payload budgets belong in
these tests so regressions fail locally. The transfer budget integration test
(`apps/server/integration/transferBudgetV2.integration.test.ts`) sends the opt-ins current clients
send and caps the decoded bytes and rows of the bounded snapshot and one older page for a 900-row
agent turn, and of the cold-connect shell for a sidebar of settled threads and idle subagents. When
clients gain an opt-in, add it to the test's client queries and give a fixture the data it saves.

## Event store and startup

Sequence cursors must seek an index rather than scan retained history. The application sequence
index contains project events and v2 thread events; the per-thread sequence index contains only v2
thread events. Legacy-only and unknown threads must return zero without scanning other threads.
Catch-up queries keep sequence ranges and optional thread or command predicates indexable.

Startup selects recovery candidates from current projection state before reading full thread
projections. Candidate selection includes queued runs, pending runtime requests, live provider
sessions, background work, and unfinished delegated deliveries. Archived threads still participate
where recovery requires them. Completed thread history is not loaded merely to discover that no
work remains.

Projection verification decodes canonical rows in bounded pages, including shared provider records
and fork ancestry. Rebuild replays event pages through a fixed sequence within its transaction;
it must not collect the entire event log before projecting it.

The focused regression coverage lives in `OrchestrationEventStore.sequence.test.ts`,
`ProjectionRecovery.test.ts`, and the provider runtime recovery tests under `apps/server/src`.

## Background work and navigation

The settlement worker reads active, unpinned threads without explicit settlement overrides from
`ProjectionStore.getSettlementCandidates`. It reads the latest run and user-message timestamps,
rejects active runs and pending requests, and checks background work using the same derivation as
the shell. It does not load archived histories, fork ancestry, transcript counts, or provider
sessions. The orchestrator still validates the current thread before applying settlement.

Read receipts use `ProjectionStore.getThread` to load only canonical thread metadata. A visit
advances `lastVisitedAt` monotonically without changing `updatedAt` or decoding history. Shell
queries use a covering thread/run index for item counts and a partial index for nonterminal
background items, including idle items. Latest user-message reads use an index ordered by update
time.

Command palette results keep live VCS and linked pull-request queries leased to the visible
viewport, including a small overscan region. Cached badges remain available while leases are
released. Local Git status reads skip divergence calculations; callers that need ahead/behind
counts keep the full status path. Cached fetch failures share the existing backoff and log only
the actual failed attempt. Unchanged desktop environment bootstrap reads retain their array
identity so polling does not invalidate subscribers.

# Testing

Rules for writing tests, and for asking for them in review. AGENTS.md carries the same writing rules under Verifying; change both together.

## What to test

- Test behavior that can break, such as orchestration and event-sourcing, provider protocol translation, auth and permission guards, persistence and migrations, external-format parsing, race fixes, and the logic a bug fix changed. Leave out tests for what types already guarantee, trivial logic, copy text, smoke runs, mock-call mirrors, callback wiring, and props rendered to static markup.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits.
- Test at one layer: the lowest one that fails on `main`. Do not repeat the case in a wrapper test, at each call site, or in web and mobile copies of the same logic.
- In review, ask for a missing test only when it would catch a real regression. Do not ask for one assertion per constant, label, or `switch` case. Flag a new test that breaks the rules above, and name the fix: fold it into the existing case or table, delete it, or keep one layer.
- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason, in an existing case of the module's test file where one fits), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures as their proof and no test: do not add UI tests for nitpicks, and do not ask for one in review when a capture already shows it. A server-only fix with no visible surface ships the test plus a short runtime transcript.

## Waiting for work

- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong. Concretely:
  - `it.effect` runs on a `TestClock`; `Effect.sleep` only advances through `TestClock.adjust`. `it.live` is wall-clock and only for subprocess or network fixtures.
  - No `yieldNow` or `sleep` polling loops. Await the `Deferred`, take from the `Queue`, or drain the worker.
  - No per-test timeout argument or `retry`. The project timeout is the ceiling, and flaky tests are fixed, not retried.
  - No `performance.now()` or `Date.now()` deltas. Assert on events and counts, not elapsed time.
  - Browser tests assert through `expect.element` or `vi.waitFor`, never `requestAnimationFrame` or `transitionend`.
  - `vi.mock` factories must not spread a real module that pulls in Shiki or the diff workers.
  - `it.skip` and friends need a tracking issue on the line above: `// quarantine: #1234 <why>`.
  - Lint enforces this: `t3code/no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip`, `t3code/no-frame-waits-in-browser-tests`, `t3code/no-wall-clock-in-tests`, `t3code/no-real-time-wait-in-tests`, `t3code/no-polling-loop-in-tests`.

    using _now = vi.spyOn(Date, "now").mockReturnValue(0);
    await using screen = await render(<TitleEditor onSave={onSave} />, { router: "/threads/1" });

# Web UI

## Primitives

Controls come from [`components/ui`](../../apps/web/src/components/ui).
[AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md#taste) says how to use and extend them.

Don't style a raw `<button>`, `<input>`, `<select>`, or `<textarea>` to look like a control a
primitive provides. Raw elements are right when the element isn't that control: semantic rows, tabs,
resize handles, swatches, editor surfaces, anything whose behavior or geometry differs by design.

## Styles

Style with Tailwind classes in the component that renders the element.

- Global CSS, in [`index.css`](../../apps/web/src/index.css) or any other stylesheet, is only for
  what classes on the owning component can't express: generated Markdown or imperative DOM, custom
  elements and shadow roots, animations, runtime theme variables, and browser or Electron
  integration.
- No `style={{ ... }}` or inline `<style>` for static values a class covers. Values computed at
  runtime are fine.
- Theme-only rules use `@variant dark` and `@variant light`, not `.dark` selectors.

## Composition

The composer banners are the reference.

- [`ComposerBanner.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/components/chat/ComposerBanner.tsx) exports one object
  of small slots. Slots own their classes, take `className`, and spread the rest of their props,
  merging classes with `cn`. Variants and density are props on `Root`. A slot that needs a control
  renders `Button`.
- [`ComposerBannerStack.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/components/chat/ComposerBannerStack.tsx) composes
  the slots and owns only stack behavior: priority, expand and collapse, dismiss transitions.
- Consumers are a few lines of slots, and the slots carry the styling:
  [`ComposerActivityStatus.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/components/chat/ComposerActivityStatus.tsx).

Build new UI the same way. Compose or extend a component instead of copying its markup and classes.
When a call site repeats a treatment another one already uses, make it a variant or a slot on the
shared component. A new composer banner or notice uses the `ComposerBanner` slots.

## Handlers in large components

V8 gives every closure created in one render a single shared scope. A memoized handler keeps
the scope of the render that created it, and that scope holds the other memoized values of that
render. When handlers in one component change at different times, each keeps an older scope that
holds older handlers, and old renders, with their server config and thread data, stay in memory
for as long as the component is mounted. React Compiler's memoized closures do the same.

In large, long-lived components such as `ChatView` and `ChatComposer`, write handlers as plain
functions and wrap them with [`useStableCallback`](../../apps/web/src/hooks/useStableCallback.ts)
only where they leave the component: props, hook dependency arrays, and effect or memo bodies.
Calls inside the component keep the plain function, so work that resumes after an `await` still
acts on the render it started in. A function that a child calls during render, or after an
`await`, comes from a module-level factory memoized on its inputs, so its closure keeps only
those inputs.

## React Compiler

The compiler memoizes a component or hook only when it can prove the code follows React's rules.
Anything it can't prove, such as reading a ref during render or calling `setState` from an effect,
makes it skip the whole function without a build error. Lint reports each skip as a
`react(...)` warning with the note "React Compiler skipped optimizing this component or hook".

Every file under `apps/web/src` must compile. Lint makes those rules errors there, and
`t3code/no-manual-memo` rejects `useMemo` and `useCallback`, which the compiler makes redundant;
no upstream rule bans them outright. It also rejects `"use memo"`. The compiler withholds a cache
scope when a value reaches plain function calls on both sides of a hook call. A `"use memo"`
helper forces one, but hides the ordering problem. Fix the order instead: plain uses of a value go
before the hook, or the helper is inlined. A `use*` helper that calls no hook is compiled as a
plain function and caches nothing, so a derived-value helper reads its source hook itself instead
of taking the value as an argument. `t3code/no-hookless-use-function` rejects a `use*` function
that calls no hook. Lint misses some bailouts, notably `try` with `finally` and
`throw` inside `try`, so [`reactCompilerCoverage.test.ts`](../../apps/web/src/reactCompilerCoverage.test.ts)
compiles every file and fails on any skip. Async handlers rarely need `try`: an
atom command settles into a result, so cleanup can follow the `await`. `useStableCallback` still
marks handlers that leave a large component, as described above.
====
# Architecture

T3 Code keeps execution in the environment that owns the workspace. Web, desktop, and mobile
clients control it over authenticated RPC. A remote client must never substitute its own filesystem,
provider credentials, or machine state for the environment's. The desktop app bundles a server,
but its renderer follows the same boundary.

## Ownership boundaries

Provider processes, terminals, Git, and project files belong to the server. Shared connection and
domain state belongs in `packages/client-runtime`; clients supply platform services and UI.
Keeping that logic shared prevents reconnect and multi-environment behavior from diverging between
web and mobile. See [connection runtime](./connection-runtime.md) and
[remote environments](./remote.md).

The [RPC contract](../../packages/contracts/src/rpc.ts) is the boundary between independently
versioned clients and servers. Subscriptions send the state a client needs, so a client viewing one
thread does not pay for every thread's history. Authentication of a socket does not authorize every
method on it. See [environment auth](./environment-auth.md).

### Pull request linking compatibility

Every protocol-2 environment advertises `threadPullRequests`. Once an environment's server config
has loaded, clients use persisted `pullRequests[]`, multi-link commands, stack UI, and reverse thread
lookup. Before that, they hide linking actions.

Environments keep advertising `threadPullRequestLinking`, accepting legacy metadata commands, and
emitting the derived `linkedPullRequest` field, because older clients still read them. That
hostless field includes only links in the thread project's own repository. Retain the legacy wire
fields, projection column, and replay support.

Provider-specific behavior belongs behind an adapter. Orchestration works with normalized commands
and events, so adding a provider should not require branches throughout the domain or clients.
See [provider constraints](./providers.md).

## Settings ownership

Client preferences stay in the current client; environment defaults and project overrides stay
on their owning server. The web and desktop settings target is URL state, resolved against current
connections and project membership. An unavailable target must not fall back to another environment.
**All environments** is an explicit bulk edit of connected, loaded servers, not a durable global
default or a promise to synchronize offline or future environments. Project-group targets similarly
select known environment-local checkouts; the group itself does not store inherited defaults.

## Durable intent and side effects

The event log is the source of truth for orchestration state. The
[v2 orchestrator](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts) serializes commands and
decides events without performing provider or filesystem work.
[EventSink](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/EventSink.ts) commits events, persisted projections,
the accepted command receipt, and outbox effects in one database transaction. Subscribers receive
events after that commit. This keeps command retries idempotent and prevents a persisted projection
from getting ahead of the event log.

The [effect worker](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/EffectWorker.ts) performs side effects
after intent has been recorded, then feeds results back into orchestration. A command acknowledgement
therefore means the intent committed, not that the provider, checkpoint, or other follow-up work
finished. Keep external I/O out of command decisions and the database transaction. Effects tied to
a lost provider process cannot simply replay; recovery retires them before admitting new work.

[v2 orchestrator](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts) serializes commands and
decides events without performing provider or filesystem work.
[EventSink](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/EventSink.ts) commits events, persisted projections,
the accepted command receipt, and outbox effects in one database transaction. Subscribers receive
events after that commit. This keeps command retries idempotent and prevents a persisted projection
from getting ahead of the event log.

The [effect worker](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/EffectWorker.ts) performs side effects
after intent has been recorded, then feeds results back into orchestration. A command acknowledgement
therefore means the intent committed, not that the provider, checkpoint, or other follow-up work
finished. Keep external I/O out of command decisions and the database transaction. Effects tied to
a lost provider process cannot simply replay; recovery retires them before admitting new work.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths-ignore:
      # Docs carry no executable code — skip CI entirely
      # when a push only touches these (mixed code+docs pushes still run).
      # Automation config (.entire/) is deliberately NOT ignored: runner
      # prompts execute in automation, so those changes must run checks.
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"
  pull_request:
    paths-ignore:
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    name: Detect changes
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      frontend: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.frontend }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
          # Full history so the path filter diffs the real change set.
          # A shallow checkout can yield an empty diff and silently skip jobs.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Filter changed paths
        id: filter
        # Pinned to the v4 tag commit: this job gates security checks, so a
        # hijacked floating tag must not be able to falsify filter outputs.
        uses: dorny/paths-filter@ceb8a2b8f2d89434be7ff52d3de7ec3738c5cc9d # v4.0.3
        with:
          # For PR synchronize events, compare only the newest push with the
          # previous head. The default PR diff compares the whole PR to main,
          # which makes a docs-only follow-up rerun code checks.
          token: ''
          base: ${{ github.event.before || github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
          predicate-quantifier: some-with-excludes
          filters: |
            frontend:
              - 'src/**'
              - 'public/**'
              - '!src/seedPersonal.ts'
              - '!public/seed-demo/**'
              - 'benchmarks/**'
              - 'electron/**'
              - 'scripts/**'
              - '.vscode/**'
              - '*.json'
              - '*.jsonc'
              - 't3.json'
              # Workspaces the root tsconfig does not cover.
              - 'extension/**'
              - 'packages/**'
              - '!packages/**/node_modules/**'
              - 'index.html'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'bun.lock'
              - '.bun-version'
              - 'vite.config.ts'
              - 'knip.json'
              - '.oxlintrc.json'
              - '.oxfmtrc.json'
              - 'oxlint-plugin-inkling/**'
              - 'tsconfig.json'
              - 'tsconfig.node.json'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'

  frontend:
    name: Frontend checks
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.frontend == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Bun
        uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with:
          bun-version-file: .bun-version

      # Guards against the three Bun pins drifting apart: .bun-version,
      # packageManager, and the Bun that setup-bun actually installed.
      - name: Verify Bun version pin
        run: bun run check:bun-version

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: bun install --frozen-lockfile

      # Root tsconfig only includes src, so the extension and shared packages
      # are invisible to `bun run typecheck`. Check each workspace explicitly.
      - name: Typecheck workspaces
        run: |
          bun run typecheck
          bun run --cwd extension typecheck
          bun run --cwd packages/ingestion-shared typecheck
          bun run --cwd packages/contracts typecheck

      - name: 'Canary: real tsc typecheck (non-blocking)'
        if: always()
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          bun run typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd extension typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd packages/ingestion-shared typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd packages/contracts typecheck:tsc

      - name: Check documented commands exist
        run: bun run check:refs

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: bun test

      - name: Check for unused code
        run: bun run knip

      - name: Lint and format frontend
        run: bun run lint

      - name: Build frontend
        run: bun run build

      # Runs the app-mode build, whose guard fails if the committed demo seed
      # has leaked back into a shipped bundle. Without this the exclusion is
      # only checked at release time.
      - name: Build frontend for the app
        run: bun run build:app

      - name: Run ingestion smoke tests
        run: bun run ingest:smoke

      # Building the Chrome MV3 extension here catches manifest and bundler
      # regressions long before someone tries to load the unpacked directory.
      - name: Build browser extension
        run: bun run --cwd extension build

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths-ignore:
      # Docs carry no executable code — skip CI entirely
      # when a push only touches these (mixed code+docs pushes still run).
      # Automation config (.entire/) is deliberately NOT ignored: runner
      # prompts execute in automation, so those changes must run checks.
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"
  pull_request:
    paths-ignore:
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    name: Detect changes
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      frontend: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.frontend }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
          # Full history so the path filter diffs the real change set.
          # A shallow checkout can yield an empty diff and silently skip jobs.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Filter changed paths
        id: filter
        # Pinned to the v4 tag commit: this job gates security checks, so a
        # hijacked floating tag must not be able to falsify filter outputs.
        uses: dorny/paths-filter@ceb8a2b8f2d89434be7ff52d3de7ec3738c5cc9d # v4.0.3
        with:
          # For PR synchronize events, compare only the newest push with the
          # previous head. The default PR diff compares the whole PR to main,
          # which makes a docs-only follow-up rerun code checks.
          token: ''
          base: ${{ github.event.before || github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
          predicate-quantifier: some-with-excludes
          filters: |
            frontend:
              - 'src/**'
              - 'public/**'
              - '!src/seedPersonal.ts'
              - '!public/seed-demo/**'
              - 'benchmarks/**'
              - 'electron/**'
              - 'scripts/**'
              - '.vscode/**'
              - '*.json'
              - '*.jsonc'
              - 't3.json'
              # Workspaces the root tsconfig does not cover.
              - 'extension/**'
              - 'packages/**'
              - '!packages/**/node_modules/**'
              - 'index.html'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'bun.lock'
              - '.bun-version'
              - 'vite.config.ts'
              - 'knip.json'
              - '.oxlintrc.json'
              - '.oxfmtrc.json'
              - 'oxlint-plugin-inkling/**'
              - 'tsconfig.json'
              - 'tsconfig.node.json'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'

  frontend:
    name: Frontend checks
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.frontend == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Bun
        uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with:
          bun-version-file: .bun-version

      # Guards against the three Bun pins drifting apart: .bun-version,
      # packageManager, and the Bun that setup-bun actually installed.
      - name: Verify Bun version pin
        run: bun run check:bun-version

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: bun install --frozen-lockfile

      # Root tsconfig only includes src, so the extension and shared packages
      # are invisible to `bun run typecheck`. Check each workspace explicitly.
      - name: Typecheck workspaces
        run: |
          bun run typecheck
          bun run --cwd extension typecheck
          bun run --cwd packages/ingestion-shared typecheck
          bun run --cwd packages/contracts typecheck

      - name: 'Canary: real tsc typecheck (non-blocking)'
        if: always()
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          bun run typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd extension typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd packages/ingestion-shared typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd packages/contracts typecheck:tsc

      - name: Check documented commands exist
        run: bun run check:refs

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: bun test

      - name: Check for unused code
        run: bun run knip

      - name: Lint and format frontend
        run: bun run lint

      - name: Build frontend
        run: bun run build

      # Runs the app-mode build, whose guard fails if the committed demo seed
      # has leaked back into a shipped bundle. Without this the exclusion is
      # only checked at release time.
      - name: Build frontend for the app
        run: bun run build:app

      - name: Run ingestion smoke tests
        run: bun run ingest:smoke

      # Building the Chrome MV3 extension here catches manifest and bundler
      # regressions long before someone tries to load the unpacked directory.
      - name: Build browser extension
        run: bun run --cwd extension build

I'm checking how much Effect is actually used in our electron code to see if a docs/internals/effect-services.md would be worthwhile. Evals seem not applicable since we're not model-facing beyond embeddings, and the knip.jsonc setup looks fine as-is. The `check:changed` script stands out as genuinely valuable though -- a script running oxlint/oxfmt and targeted tests only on changed files would address how slow our full check command is, which matches what AGENTS.md already asks for in spirit but doesn't automate. I'm also noting their test-hygiene lint rules (banning fixed sleeps, wall-clock checks, polling loops) mirror text already in our AGENTS.md, but ours isn't lint-enforced -- though checking scale, only one test file actually violates this, so it may not be worth the tooling investment yet.

I want to check how many useEffect hooks we actually have before deciding if `no-unreasoned-state-sync` is worth adopting, since it could flag a lot of noise. I should also check whether we use React Compiler already, since `no-manual-memo` only makes sense alongside that. The `agent-context-budget` rule doesn't apply since our AGENTS.md is already comparable in size to theirs, and PR size labeling seems low-value for a single-dev-plus-agents repo. Finally, I'm weighing whether any of our trickier systems -- job queue leases, asset path containment, electron preload IPC contracts, performance regression guards -- deserve a dedicated internal doc despite our stated preference not to spin up a separate docs/internals tree yet.

A dedicated performance doc with explicit budgets and invariants seems like a genuinely good idea, especially IPC payload size tests to ensure we send summaries rather than full content -- I should grep for existing payload tests since I suspect there aren't any. I also want to check our packages/contracts setup and whether the electron preload bridge types are hand-duplicated or derived from the schema contracts, since that's a key "surface" area worth tightening.

Looking at worktree tooling, I'm comparing their setup-worktree script and DB-seeding approach against ours, and want to verify whether we actually have a script for copying the SQLite database with proper backup semantics versus just describing it in docs. I'm also noting that running multiple worktrees concurrently could cause Vite dev server port collisions since 5173 isn't guaranteed unique -- their port-derivation-from-worktree-path approach is a nice stability feature worth checking against our vite.config.ts, though it's a minor concern.

I'm now digging into their CI setup since it runs on ubuntu-24.04 despite our app being Windows-only Electron -- this seems like a real gap since path-containment and native dialog tests on Linux use posix semantics and don't actually validate Windows behavior. I want to check release.yml and electron-preview.yml to see if there's a dedicated Windows test job we're missing, since AGENTS.md claims CI covers "Electron package smoke tests" but ci.yml only shows the frontend job running on ubuntu. I also note they use dependabot, security scanning, and link checking, which we have equivalents for, and that their vite-plus toolchain isn't worth switching to since we've already standardized on bun, oxlint, oxfmt, and tsc-rs.

I'm now comparing their apps/web structure against ours -- their UI primitives setup versus our src/ui -- and want to look at several of their lint rules against our codebase: checking for native title tooltips we could replace with our custom Tooltip component, scanning for unscoped `:has()` CSS selectors that could hurt performance in card grids, and checking resize observer usage. I also want to peek at their consistency-action-names doc since it might relate to our own entry-point naming concerns, then check their package.json scripts and lint config around line 207 to see which specific rules they've enabled.
