docs/tech-stack.md:19:| Application core | Electron main process and Node.js, in TypeScript on Effect | File, job queue, database, and model-process orchestration |
docs/tech-stack.md:20:| IPC contract | `@inkling/contracts` command list and Effect Schemas | Preload, main process, and renderer share one command list; arguments are decoded before storage sees them |
docs/tech-stack.md:21:| Database | SQLite through `@effect/sql-sqlite-node`, with migrations on `node:sqlite` | Typed queries and transactions over one serialized connection; migrations and FTS5 stay plain SQL |
docs/tech-stack.md:24:| Background work | Effect workers over a job queue persisted in SQLite | Retryable processing without blocking the UI |
docs/tech-stack.md:26:## Effect in the main process
docs/tech-stack.md:28:The main process is built on [Effect](https://effect.website) so leases, timeouts, retries, and shutdown come from one tested runtime instead of hand-rolled timers and flags. `electron/main.ts` builds a single `ManagedRuntime` holding the library, the job queue, and two workers; quitting disposes it, which interrupts running jobs and hands them back as pending. Each job kind has a timeout in `electron/ai-jobs.ts`, so a hung model or decoder fails its job instead of stalling the queue. Effect stops at the IPC edge: handlers call storage through a Promise facade, and the renderer never imports Effect at runtime.
docs/tech-stack.md:30:URL ingestion downloads through Effect's HTTP client, which retries rate limits, gateway errors, and dropped connections, waits at least as long as a `Retry-After` header asks, and stays inside the 15-second capture budget. Redirects stay manual so each hop passes the private-network check before it is followed.
AGENTS.md:37:The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here. Most work in this repo will be done by agents, sometimes remote. Be careful with data, dev servers, and anything that could damage the session you are working from.

This documentation covers the Effect library and its related packages.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that `isInside` relies on path logic that differs by platform, but the CI only tests POSIX semantics on Linux while the actual app ships on Windows with its own path quirks—meaning the Windows-only installer job never actually runs the tests, leaving a real coverage gap.

Separately, AGENTS.md's "Where code lives" section is stale: it still references App.tsx as central when the real code has moved into feature folders, and it omits newer packages like `packages/contracts`, `packages/ingestion-shared`, `extension/`, and `electron/storage/` entirely.

I also want to check the Effect usage pattern — grepping for `Effect.fn(` vs `Effect.gen` shows the codebase relies entirely on `Effect.gen` with zero `Effect.fn` usage, which might be worth flagging as an optional convention since the Effect docs lean toward `Effect.fn` for reusable functions, though I won't dig deeper into that.

On test hygiene, AGENTS.md already prohibits sleeps, wall-clock deltas, per-test timeouts, and unreasoned skips in prose, and a grep confirms zero current violations except a benign Promise wrapper in native-dialog.test. Since the codebase is already clean, it'd be cheap to lock this in with 2-3 lint rules (no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip, no-wall-clock-in-tests, no-real-time-wait-in-tests), porting simplified versions of the TS/effect-based rules rather than depending directly on those packages.

I'm weighing whether this is worth the moderate effort given yagni principles and the already-clean state, but since this is largely an agent-driven repo and other projects got burned by drift, I'd rank it medium-low priority.

Next, the `check:changed` script feels high-value: a single command that composes targeted lint, format-check, and test runs for just the changed files (with sibling test mapping like foo.ts → foo.test.ts) plus knip, caching identical-state reruns, kept lean at roughly 60 lines rather than something bloated.

Then there's the Windows test lane already noted, and performance invariants as pinned tests so payload budget regressions get caught rather than drifting silently.

Checking whether we already pin IPC payload shapes in tests, I find storage.test.ts already asserts that content doesn't leak into card summaries, and there's a bench script for the library grid — so this is already partially covered and probably just needs a brief mention rather than new documentation.

On docs structure, we intentionally skip a large internals tree unlike other projects, but I'm noticing there's no dedicated user guide directory despite AGENTS.md calling for user-facing docs in the product's voice — it's a small inconsistency worth flagging.

Going through what from t3code I wouldn't adopt — vite-plus, pnpm, Effect RPC for IPC, the various bot/triage tooling, evals, vendoring — React Compiler stands out as the one plausible item, given the codebase has 138 manual memoization-related hook calls. I'll list it as worth a future spike rather than a firm recommendation.

For the lint rules they enable that we've disabled (react/refs, set-state-in-effect, immutability, exhaustive-effect-dependencies, purity), I want a concrete data point rather than speculation, so I'll run a targeted, read-only oxlint pass on src with those rules turned on to count actual violations — this stays within the read-only/no-repo-wide-checks constraint since it's scoped and non-destructive. I'll pair that with a quick count of existing useMemo/useCallback usage for comparison.

content.text:
Our setup already matches t3code's on most points. We've adopted its `AGENTS.md` structure, oxlint and oxfmt, the comment and suppression-reason rules, knip, and tsc-rs. We also have a few things it lacks, like `check:refs` and the contracts package for IPC. So the gap is small. I made no changes. I read t3code in a scratch clone outside the worktree, and the one lint run on our `src` was read-only.

## Worth doing, in order

1. **`AGENTS.md` has a stale code map.** It says the library grid, cards and Spaces UI live in `src/App.tsx`. They live in `src/features/library`, `src/features/spaces` and `src/features/shell`. `App.tsx` is a 779-line wiring file. The map also omits `packages/contracts` (the IPC command list), `packages/ingestion-shared`, `extension/` (an entry point) and `scripts/`. Agents follow this map, so it's the cheapest fix with the biggest effect.

2. **Add `bun run check:changed`.** t3code has one script that runs lint, format, knip, typecheck and the sibling tests for just the changed files. Our `AGENTS.md` asks agents to assemble that by hand, and `bun run check` is too heavy for that. A trimmed version of about 60 lines would do: `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on changed files, plus `bun test` for `foo.test.ts` next to a changed `foo.ts`.

3. **Run tests on Windows in CI.** The `frontend` job runs `bun test` on `ubuntu-24.04`. The Windows jobs only build the installer. Asset containment (`isInside` in `electron/storage/shared.ts`) depends on `node:path` separators. The traversal test therefore only proves POSIX behavior, while the app ships on Windows. t3code has a Windows test lane, though only on manual dispatch. I'd run `bun test electron/` on `windows-latest`. I haven't confirmed the suite passes there in CI, though it's developed on Windows.

4. **Tell agents where Effect's docs are.** `electron/` is built on Effect 4.0.6, and `AGENTS.md` never mentions it. That version ships its own `AGENTS.md` and `ai-docs/` in `node_modules/effect`, so t3code's vendored `.repos/effect-smol` isn't needed. One pointer line is enough. Effect's guidance prefers `Effect.fn("name")` for reusable functions, and our `electron/` has no `Effect.fn(` calls. Treat that as optional.

5. **Turn on the React rules we've disabled.** t3code runs `set-state-in-effect`, `refs`, `immutability` and `exhaustive-effect-dependencies` as errors. We have them off. Enabling them gives 25 diagnostics in 14 files: 13 `set-state-in-effect`, 8 `refs`, 2 `immutability` and 2 `exhaustive-effect-dependencies`. These are mostly cascading-render patterns, which fits the performance principle. `react/purity` has zero hits and isn't in our config, so it can go on today.

6. **Lint the test rules that `AGENTS.md` only states in prose.** t3code enforces no sleeps, no wall-clock deltas, no per-test timeouts and no skips without a reason. We have zero violations today, so this guards against drift rather than fixing anything. Port two or three of the rules only if agents start regressing.

## Skip

- **Tooling and release machinery:** the `vite-plus` and pnpm toolchain, the provider package split, PR-size labels, and the vouch and triage bots.
- **`agent-context-budget` workflow:** it budgets the prompt text t3code injects into agents, not `AGENTS.md`.
- **`evals/`:** we have no model-facing text.
- **`docs/internals/` tree:** our `docs/README.md` defers it on purpose.
- **React Compiler with `no-manual-memo`:** we have 55 manual memo sites. t3code's docs say bailouts are silent and need a coverage test to catch them, so at most a spike.

Items 1, 2 and 4 are small and could go in one change. Item 5 is a separate cleanup. Tell me which to start on.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

<runtime_info>In case you're asked: you are running in T3 Code through the Claude Code harness. No need to mention this otherwise. You can embed images, video, and audio in your response using Markdown image syntax with absolute file paths. Link any other file you produce using its absolute path so the user can open it in T3 Code's files viewer.</runtime_info>

<pull_request_linking>
Link each PR you create, take over, or push to: one link_pull_request per PR, full URL, every stack layer, as your next call. Host tools do not link for you. If linking fails, say so. Skip PRs you only read or review, and PRs named only as background. Call watch_pull_request when asked to monitor or babysit, or when work you were asked to do, such as a merge, still waits on checks or reviews, even after an earlier unwatch. Finish any needed branch update and push first, then watch and end your turn. Otherwise act now or hand back. Delegated children never watch, even if the brief says babysit. After PR work, a child's last line is: PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>. Links and watches persist across pushes. Never wait with sleep, loops, gh --watch, Monitor, or ScheduleWakeup. Before handback, call unwatch_pull_request on any PR you watch.
</pull_request_linking>

## T3 Code orchestration

Ordinary coding tasks need no T3 tools.

- Subagents: use your native tool when the child uses your provider, a model it offers, and no settings beyond yours, and it finishes in this turn (Claude `Agent` always with `run_in_background:false`; Codex `spawn_agent`, then wait). Use `delegate_task` for another provider's model, user-asked settings, a separate checkout (`isolation:"worktree"`), background work, or `delegate_task` by name. A native type running another provider's model counts too. Workflow only when asked.
- Call `orchestrator_capabilities` once per thread, before the first `delegate_task`. Again only after an error or a user-named provider change. Settings go in `target.options`. Provider or model unavailable: say so. Never switch unasked, or fall back to native tools, Workflow, or CLIs. Never make a child's checkout in the shell or in `task`.
- Every new delegate review or re-check is a new `delegate_task` (brief, findings, objections), never a `t3_thread_send`. Fix small review findings yourself; start no delegate for them. When told to proceed without a delegate, or to run fewer, `task_cancel` the extras. Start no replacement.
- Follow a running delegate's `next`. Do not poll it (`task_status`, `sleep`, watchers, Monitor, ScheduleWakeup). Stop a delegate run you replace or no longer need with `task_cancel`, never `t3_thread_interrupt` on a `childThreadId`.
- If you are a subagent or child, do the work yourself. Start no subagents unless your task says to.

- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` make new top-level threads, only when the user asks for a new thread. "Subagent", "delegate", and "parallel" never mean one. Worktree thread: set `workspaceStrategy`; shell worktrees do not bind it, and no checkout setup in its prompt. No `workspaceStrategy`: project root, not your worktree.
- Given a thread id, `t3_thread_read` it before you answer about it.
- Another machine: `t3_environment_links` lists linked ones. Pass its `environmentId` to a T3 tool to act there. Ids are then that machine's, so pass `threadId`.
- A machine the user names that is not linked ("delegate this to my vps"): call `t3_environment_link` with a `hint` from their words. Never ask for a pairing code in chat.
- In your reply, mention a thread by its `link`, verbatim. Never a plain title or bare id.
- A secret: call `request_secret` yourself. Pass its `secretRef` to a T3 tool, or use `delivery: "file"` for a shell command. Never ask in chat or invent one. When asked only to schedule, `schedule_task` without running its prompt.
- T3 tools may load late. Try the name once before you call it absent.

### Visuals and preview

- Answer data with a trend or comparison with a chart, and show any visual the user asks for here: pass its HTML to `html_preview`, then `html_render`. If the visual is a file, pass that file's HTML. A screenshot on disk or a text description does not show it. Never start a server for it. Tools a web page exposes give data only. Never use them to show results. Asked for an image to post, send, or use elsewhere: a `.png` file and its path, never `html_render`.
- Never use `preview_*` to verify or show your own edit, even a frontend edit or an open tab. Do not repeat preview calls from an earlier turn. Use them only when the current request asks for browser work or names a page or tab. Public pages: web fetch or search unless browser work was asked; then preview tools only, no web fetch. Close a tab you opened before you reply, unless the user asked for it or uses it.


### Background work you wait on

To wait for a background command or Monitor you started (tests, a build), call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID before you end your turn. Do not mark work you leave running, or PRs. T3 MCP tools are deferred: load one with ToolSearch before you call it.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

input.title: Fix stale code map in AGENTS.md
input.task:
You are working in the inkling repo (Electron + React + TypeScript + SQLite, Windows app). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it (docs rules, PR rules, the "three ways to hurt yourself", no repo-wide checks). Do the work yourself; do not start subagents.

## Goal
The "Where code lives" section of AGENTS.md is stale and sends agents to the wrong files. Fix it with the smallest accurate edit. Docs-only change.

## Known problems (verify each against the code before writing; do not trust this list blindly)
1. The `src/components/` bullet says "The library grid, cards, and Spaces UI live in `src/App.tsx`, and the reader is `src/ReaderView.tsx`." In reality the app is organised by feature under `src/features/` (capture, item-view, library, settings, shell, spaces). The library grid/cards are in `src/features/library/` (e.g. LibraryStage.tsx, LibraryCard.tsx), the expanded item overlay and PDF viewer are in `src/features/item-view/`, Spaces logic is in `src/features/spaces/` plus `src/features/shell/SpacesSection.tsx`. `src/App.tsx` is only the top-level wiring of those features. `src/components/` holds shared pieces (ItemMedia.tsx, LiquidGlass, mascot, onboarding, etc.). `src/ReaderView.tsx` still exists; confirm.
2. The section omits places an agent needs to know about: `packages/contracts` (the IPC command list and Effect Schemas shared by preload, main and renderer; see docs/tech-stack.md), `packages/ingestion-shared`, `extension/` (the browser extension, itself a capture entry point), `scripts/`, and `electron/storage/` (SQLite storage and job queue; confirm the layout). Check `src/lib/`, `src/ui/` too and mention only what is useful.
3. Check every other path named in the "Where code lives" section still exists and is described accurately (`src/lib/ingestion/`, `benchmarks/`, `public/seed-demo/`, `src/seedPersonal.ts`, `docs/`, `oxlint-plugin-inkling/` if mentioned). Fix anything else that is wrong.

## Constraints
- Edit only the "Where code lives" section of AGENTS.md unless you find another factually wrong path reference elsewhere in the file; then fix that too and say so in the PR.
- Keep it short: one line per location, no file catalogs, no enumerating every file. The AGENTS.md documentation rules apply: add only what a maintainer/agent would get wrong without it. Match the existing voice and formatting.
- Do not touch docs/changelog.md (trivial doc fix; AGENTS.md says trivial edits skip the changelog). Never mention an agent did the work in docs.
- Do not start dev servers or the Electron app. No full test/typecheck runs. Verify by reading the repo (ls, grep) that every path you wrote exists. `bun run check:refs` (scripts/assert-command-refs.ts) validates command references in docs; run it if it is cheap and relevant.
- Create a branch from the current HEAD named `docs/agents-code-map` (you are in your own worktree).

## Delivery (full-stop: PR ready for the user to merge, but you NEVER merge)
- Commit with a conventional title, e.g. `docs(agents): correct the code map in AGENTS.md`. End the commit message with the line: `Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- Fetch origin, rebase onto the latest origin/main, push the branch, and open a PR with `gh` (use the `file-pr` skill if you have it). PR body: the problem in a sentence or two (stale paths in the code map), then what you changed, one short line saying how you verified (every path checked on disk). End the body with: `Claude Haiku 5.5 (T3 Code)` and then `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.
- Never merge, enable auto-merge, enter a merge queue, push to main, or bypass protections. Do not call watch_pull_request. If checks run (CI skips docs-only pushes by design), look once at their state and report it; do not poll or sleep.
- If a bot or CI finding appears while you are still active, fix real ones and push; otherwise just report state.
- Your final message's last line must be exactly: `PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>`. Before it, list in 3-6 lines what you changed and anything you were unsure about.

For the lint rules explanation, I want to make clear that AGENTS.md currently only describes these constraints in prose—no fixed sleeps, per-test timeouts, retries, timing deltas, unreasoned skips—whereas dedicated lint rules would catch violations mechanically via oxlint instead of relying on reviewers. I'm describing what each rule would flag: hardcoded test timeouts or unexplained skips, wall-clock timing calls in test files, real-time waits like setTimeout, and polling loops that sleep until a condition is met. This matters especially for job queue lease/recovery tests, which are exactly where agents tend to reach for sleep-based hacks; I grepped the codebase and found it currently clean aside from one Promise wrapper that isn't actually a sleep, though I'll admit I only grepped rather than reading every test closely.

Given the cost of implementing a 30-60 line AST rule and the fact our plugin only has two rules so far, I'm leaning toward deprioritizing this—either skip it until a regression occurs or just implement the skip/timeout rule alone, since the user asked for items 4 and 5, not 6.

The critical catch is that the compiler silently bails out on any component violating React's rules (reading refs during render, calling setState in effects, try/finally blocks) without throwing a build error—it just skips memoizing that component silently. I handed item 1 to Claude Haiku 5.5 at xhigh effort in its own worktree. It's fixing the stale `AGENTS.md` code map and opening a PR. Per full-stop, it won't merge, and I'll link the PR here when it reports back. The rest of your questions:

**2: `check:changed` vs the full suite.** Yes. `check:changed` is the fast check you run while iterating and before you push, and it covers only what your diff touches, so it takes seconds. `bun run check` mirrors the CI frontend job and runs everything, including installs and both builds. CI stays the full gate. One limit: it maps tests by filename (`foo.ts` runs `foo.test.ts`), so a change to a shared helper won't run the tests of distant callers. CI catches those.

**6: test-hygiene lint rules.**
- **What we have now:** `AGENTS.md` says in prose to use no fixed sleeps, no per-test timeouts or retries, no `Date.now()` or `performance.now()` deltas, and no skips without a reason. Nothing enforces it.
- **What the rules do:** they turn each of those into a lint error. For example, `test("x", fn, 5000)` or a bare `.skip` fails lint, as does `Date.now()` inside a `*.test.ts`. A `while` loop that sleeps until a condition is true also fails.
- **Why it matters here:** the job queue lease and recovery tests are where an agent most often reaches for a sleep or a timing assertion, and those tests then flake under CI load.
- **Where we stand:** I grepped the tests and found no skips, `.only`, timeout arguments or sleeps. The one `new Promise` in `electron/native-dialog.test.ts` is a wrapper, not a wait. I didn't read every test.
- **Cost and recommendation:** each rule is a 30–60 line visitor in our plugin, which has two rules today. Since the tests are clean, I'd skip this until an agent regresses. If you want one now, take the skip-and-timeout rule.

**React Compiler and `no-manual-memo`.**
- **What it is:** the compiler is a build step that memoizes components and hooks automatically. With it on, `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo` are redundant, so t3code bans them with `no-manual-memo`. We have 55 manual memo sites and no compiler.
- **The catch:** if a component breaks React's rules, the compiler skips it silently, with no build error, and it just goes unmemoized. t3code needs lint rules at error level plus a test that compiles every file and fails on any skip. Even then, its docs say lint misses some skips. They also describe a memory trap in large long-lived components.
- **How it ties to item 5:** reading refs during render and calling `setState` in effects are exactly what makes the compiler bail. Our 8 `refs` and 13 `set-state-in-effect` diagnostics would be the files it skips. So fix item 5 first.
- **Recommendation:** after item 5, run a spike on a branch. Enable the compiler, count how many files bail, and compare scroll performance with `scripts/bench-library-grid.mjs`. I haven't checked how it would plug into our Vite and oxc setup, so that's part of the spike.

**Queued:** 3 (Windows CI), 4 (Effect pointer) and 5 (React rules) are approved but not started, because you only assigned item 1. They'd be separate PRs under our one-request-one-PR rule. Item 4 edits `AGENTS.md`, so I'd wait for the item 1 PR to land to avoid a conflict. Items 3 and 5 can start any time. For 3, say if you want the whole frontend job moved to `windows-latest` or only the tests. I'd move everything, since the app is Windows-only, and keep the Linux Xvfb smoke job as is.

content.content:
## Dev servers

- `bun install` installs. If module resolution looks broken, run `bun run check:bun-version`.
- `bun run dev` is the quick web look at the UI. It uses sample data and has no desktop storage or processing backend.
- `bun run dev:app` opens the Electron shell in preview mode. The renderer shows the sample library and does not call the desktop backend, so capture, OCR, embeddings, and local file access are not exercised there. Test the full backend with the packaged output of `bun run build:dir`.
- `t3.json` lists the T3 Code run scripts. Keep it up to date: whenever a package.json script is renamed or removed, or a command it runs changes, update `t3.json` in the same change.
- Ports and state come from the dev setup, not from memory. Read the actual terminal output. Do not assume a port.
- Stop what you started, by the handle you tracked. See rule 1.
- Never `Start-Sleep` (or any blocking wait) after launching a server. Start it detached, do other work, then poll its log or port. A sleep blocks you from doing anything else while you wait.

## Test data

An empty library is a bad test. Seed your run with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state.

- Copy the database file with SQLite backup semantics so the copy is consistent even if the source app is open. A raw file copy of a live database is a corrupt copy. Bring the `-wal` and `-shm` siblings when you copy raw, or better, back up through the engine.
- Data flows one way. Into your sandbox, never back out. Copy in, never symlink. Never write your test edits back to the source.
- Bring assets only for the items your flow needs. Do not copy the whole asset store to test one card.
- The committed demo seed in `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the safe default for UI work. It shuffles with a fixed seed so the order is mixed but stable. Prefer it over real data when it covers your case.
- Never commit a copied database, a real user item, or a downloaded model. The gitignore already excludes run artifacts. Keep it that way.

## Verifying

- Smallest proof that the change works: `bun test <files>` for the tests you touched, `bunx oxlint <files>` and `bunx oxfmt --check <files>` for what you changed, and `bun run typecheck` (fast enough to run whole). The full check is `bun run check`, which mirrors the CI frontend job. Do not run it unless you changed something broad or the user asked.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No full `bun test` sweep or full `tsc` unless asked. CI owns the full suite.
- A test earns its place by guarding something that breaks quietly: extraction and sanitizing, embed allowlists, OCR scoring, queue leases and recovery, migrations and persistence, asset path containment and range requests, deep link and external-format parsing, ordering and race guarantees, and `liquidGlassShape`. A test added with a bug fix stays; mark it `// regression: #NNN` if its name doesn't say so.
- Don't write tests the types already prove, trivial logic, basic DOM behavior, static-markup renders, mock-call mirrors, smoke tests, duplicate table rows, or wall-clock and perf asserts.
- Ingestion and background changes ship with focused tests for that behavior. A behavior change with no test is unfinished.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures and no test.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits. Test at the lowest layer that fails on `main`, not again in a wrapper or at each call site.
- Background work is async. Await the real signal: a job drain, a lease state, an event. No fixed sleeps, per-test timeouts, retries, `Date.now()` or `performance.now()` deltas, polling loops, or skips without a reason.
- UI changes need one real pass in the running app before you call them done (the `verify-inkling` skill drives it). Preview for layout, full app for anything native. Take a screenshot through the harness so the user can see it. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Clean up what you launched when you are done.
- There are no local hooks. CI runs the frontend checks and Electron package smoke tests.

## Pull requests
## How it works

Capture creates the item immediately, then background jobs do the slow parts. Normalize, extract text and metadata, run OCR or PDF extraction or article parsing, generate embeddings. Writes to items update the FTS index through triggers. The user keeps browsing or does something else while jobs run. A job can be retried, its lease can expire, and interrupted jobs recover on restart.

Search combines exact FTS over content, notes, and OCR text with semantic similarity over local embeddings. Smart Spaces are saved searches whose query runs each time their items load, so they need no background job.

The Electron main process owns files, the job queue, the database, and model execution. The renderer gets a narrow preload bridge, not raw filesystem or shell access. Fetched HTML is untrusted. It gets sanitized, embeds pass an allowlist, scripts and event handlers are stripped.

Full reasoning in `docs/tech-stack.md`. Behavior contract in `docs/product-behavior.md`.

## Where code lives

- `src/` is the React and TypeScript frontend. Entry at `src/main.tsx`.
- `src/lib/ingestion/` is the capture and extraction pipeline. Defuddle, metadata fallback, sanitizing, video link handling.
- `src/components/` holds shared pieces such as the card media (`ItemMedia.tsx`), the expanded item overlay, and the PDF viewer. The library grid, cards, and Spaces UI live in `src/App.tsx`, and the reader is `src/ReaderView.tsx`.
- `electron/` holds the desktop main process, preload bridge, SQLite storage, job queue, PDF/OCR, embeddings, and packaging inputs.
- `benchmarks/` holds the corpus, the harness, expected outputs, and results. Of the results, only `results-latest.json` and `summary.md` are tracked.
- `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the committed demo library for UI work.

I'll note this interpretation choice when reporting back, and for model selection I'll let most children inherit the default model rather than specifying something smaller like Haiku.

Since delegated children can't babysit or watch CI themselves, I need to own that role — the child files the PR and reports back with the PR URL, head SHA, and check status, then I watch and merge when gates pass. For item 3 specifically, since Windows CI is the actual validation, and this machine itself runs Windows 11, I can have the child reproduce the targeted test failures locally before pushing, which sidesteps the no-polling restriction somewhat and lets me iterate on real CI failures if they occur.

For the Windows CI fix itself: switch the `frontend` job to `windows-latest` while leaving the `changes` job on ubuntu. I need to flag a subtle gotcha for the child — on Windows runners the default shell is pwsh, and multi-line `run: |` blocks there only check the exit code of the last native command, so a failing step in the middle of a multi-command block can silently pass. I should tell the child to switch those steps to `shell: bash` instead, since Git Bash on Windows runners properly fails fast on any failing command in sequence.

Repo: inkling (Electron + React + TS). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root and follow it. Do the work yourself; no subagents.

## Goal
PR #193 (https://github.com/Squidys-Tools/inkling/pull/193, branch `docs/agents-code-map`) now has merge conflicts with `main` in AGENTS.md. Resolve them and force-push the PR branch. Do NOT merge, enable auto-merge, or touch any other branch.

## Context
PR #193 rewrites only the "Where code lives" section of AGENTS.md (fixes stale paths: feature code is in `src/features/`, `src/App.tsx` only composes them; adds `packages/contracts`, `packages/ingestion-shared`, `extension/`, `scripts/`, `electron/storage/`; benchmark results path `benchmarks/results/`; real `docs/` contents). Since then main got #194 (commit 2c45127 "tighten AGENTS.md and pin Bun once in .bun-version"), which rewrote other parts of AGENTS.md and shortened a few bullets in "Where code lives" (e.g. it drops "48 item" from the benchmarks bullet and removes the "No other docs home exists yet" sentence).

## Steps
1. `git fetch origin`. The branch `docs/agents-code-map` may already be checked out in another worktree, so do not check it out by name. Create a local branch from the remote one: `git switch -c fix-193-conflicts origin/docs/agents-code-map`.
2. `git rebase origin/main`. Resolve the AGENTS.md conflict: take main's version of everything outside "Where code lives" exactly as is (#194's wording wins there). In "Where code lives", keep #193's corrections and fold in #194's intent (no stale counts, no leftover "no other docs home" sentence). The result should be one line per location, accurate, matching the surrounding voice.
3. Re-verify every path named in "Where code lives" exists on disk (ls). Run `bun run check:refs` (needs `bun install` first if node_modules is missing; the bun version must match .bun-version).
4. Push with `git push --force-with-lease origin HEAD:docs/agents-code-map`. Do not force-push anything else.
5. Check the PR once with `gh pr view 193 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus,headRefOid,statusCheckRollup`. Do not poll, sleep, or call watch_pull_request.

Your final message: 3 to 5 lines on how you resolved the conflict, then the last line exactly: `PR https://github.com/Squidys-Tools/inkling/pull/193, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>`.

input.title: Add bun run check:changed
input.task:
Repo: inkling (Electron + React + TS, Bun, Windows app). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root and follow it (verifying rules, docs rules, PR rules, the "three ways to hurt yourself"). Do the work yourself; no subagents. This machine is Windows; use Bun APIs with argument arrays, no shell string commands, and no bash-only syntax in the script.

## Goal
Add `bun run check:changed`: one command an agent or dev runs while iterating and before pushing. It runs the fast subset of CI's checks for only what the branch changed. `bun run check` (the full CI mirror) stays as is. Inspiration is t3code's `scripts/check-changed.ts` (https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/blob/main/scripts/check-changed.ts), but ours must be much smaller: yagni, aim for roughly 100 lines. Do NOT copy its run-result cache, workspace/affected-package mapping, patch check, or GraphQL parts.

## Behavior
- `bun run check:changed` compares against `git merge-base HEAD origin/main`; optional first argument is another ref. If there is no merge base, print a one-line hint to `git fetch origin` and exit 1.
- Changed files = `git diff --name-only --no-renames <base>` plus untracked files (`git ls-files --others --exclude-standard`). Only files that still exist are passed to tools. No changes -> print so and exit 0.
- Steps (run concurrently, print each step's output when it finishes, then a pass/fail summary, exit non-zero if any failed):
  1. `oxlint` on changed JS/TS files (`bunx oxlint <files>` or the local binary; match how package.json's `lint` script invokes it).
  2. `oxfmt --check` on changed files oxfmt handles. Make sure files in `.oxfmtrc.json` ignorePatterns (md, yml, bun.lock, etc.) are not passed in a way that makes oxfmt error with "no target files"; test this with a docs-only change and with an ignored file.
  3. `bun test` on changed test files plus sibling tests of changed source files (`foo.ts` -> `foo.test.ts` in the same directory; also `.test.tsx`). Skip the step when none.
  4. `bun run knip` when any code file or package.json/knip.json changed.
  5. `bun run typecheck` when any code or tsconfig/package.json changed (it is fast enough to run whole).
- Must work on Windows (backslash paths from git are forward-slash; normalize anyway) and in a git worktree.

## Also update (same change)
- `package.json`: add the `check:changed` script.
- `t3.json`: add a matching run script entry (AGENTS.md requires t3.json to stay in sync with package.json scripts).
- `AGENTS.md` "Verifying": the first bullet currently hand-composes `bun test <files>`, `bunx oxlint <files>`, `bunx oxfmt --check <files>`, `bun run typecheck`. Replace that with `bun run check:changed` as the pre-push command (keep `bun test <files>` for fast iteration and keep the "do not run repo-wide checks" rule and the note that `bun run check` mirrors CI). Edit only that bullet; do not touch "Where code lives" or "How it works" (other open PRs edit those).
- `docs/operations/development.md`: add it where the commands/checks are listed. Keep it to a line or two.
- `bun run check:refs` must pass (it validates command references in docs).
- Skip the changelog (internal dev tooling, trivial per docs rules) unless docs/changelog.md's header says otherwise.
- A test only if the file-to-test mapping has non-obvious logic; do not add trivial tests. Prove it works by running `bun run check:changed` on your own branch's changes, on a docs-only change, on an empty diff, and once with a deliberately broken lint/test change (revert it afterwards). Report the observed results.

## Delivery (full-stop: PR ready for the user, never merged by you)
- Branch from latest origin/main (`git fetch origin; git switch -c chore/check-changed origin/main`). Other PRs are open, so keep the diff to the files above.
- Conventional commit, e.g. `chore(scripts): add check:changed for fast pre-push checks`. End the commit message with your own `Co-Authored-By: <your model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>` line.
- Push and open a PR with `gh` (use the `file-pr` skill if you have it). Body: the problem in a sentence or two (agents hand-assemble checks), how you fixed it, one line on how you verified, and end with your model name and harness `(T3 Code)`, then `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.
- Never merge, enable auto-merge, or push to main. Do not call watch_pull_request; do not poll or sleep. Look at check state once.
- Last line of your final message exactly: `PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>`. Above it, 3-6 lines on what you did and any doubts.

input.title: Move frontend CI to Windows
input.task:
Repo: inkling (Electron + React + TS, Bun, Windows-only desktop app). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root and follow it. Do the work yourself; no subagents. This machine is Windows, which is the same OS CI will use, so reproduce locally instead of burning CI runs.

## Goal
The `frontend` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on `ubuntu-24.04`, so `bun test` (including asset path containment in `electron/storage/shared.ts` `isInside`, which depends on `node:path` separators) only proves POSIX behavior while the app ships on Windows. Move the `frontend` job to `windows-latest` so the full suite runs on the real target OS. input.title: Point agents at Effect 4 docs
input.task:
Repo: inkling (Electron + React + TS). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root and follow it (especially its documentation rules: add only what a maintainer would get wrong without it). Do the work yourself; no subagents. Docs-only change.

## Goal
The Electron main process is built on Effect (package `effect` 4.0.6, `@effect/sql-sqlite-node`; see docs/tech-stack.md "Effect in the main process"). AGENTS.md never tells agents that. Effect 4 differs a lot from Effect 3, which is what most model training data shows, so agents hallucinate old APIs. The installed package ships its own agent docs: `node_modules/effect/AGENTS.md` and `node_modules/effect/ai-docs/`, plus the full `src/`. Add a short pointer so agents read those instead of memory or the web.

## What to write
- Add one or two sentences to AGENTS.md in the paragraph under "How it works" that starts "The Electron main process owns files, the job queue, the database, and model execution." Say: main-process code is Effect 4 (not 3), and before writing or changing Effect code read `node_modules/effect/AGENTS.md` and `node_modules/effect/ai-docs/` and the package source rather than relying on memory. If node_modules is missing, `bun install` first.
- Do NOT edit the "Where code lives" section (another open PR rewrites it and would conflict). Do not edit anything else in AGENTS.md.
- Do not add a convention list (Effect.fn vs Effect.gen etc.); the package docs cover it and the existing code does not follow one.
- Verify before writing: that the two paths exist after `bun install` (check package.json version pin, `ls node_modules/effect`), and confirm via `electron/` that the main process really uses `effect`. Use the exact paths you saw.
- docs/changelog.md: skip (trivial docs edit). `bun run check:refs` must pass.

## Delivery (full-send, but YOU do not merge or watch; the parent agent will)
- Branch from latest origin/main (`git fetch origin; git switch -c docs/effect-docs-pointer origin/main`).
- Conventional commit, e.g. `docs(agents): point agents at the bundled Effect 4 docs`. End with your own `Co-Authored-By: <your model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- Push and open a PR with `gh` (use `file-pr` skill if you have it). Body: problem in a sentence or two, what you changed, one line on verification, end with your model name and harness `(T3 Code)`, then `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.
- Do not merge, enable auto-merge, or call watch_pull_request. No sleeping or polling; check state once.
- Last line of your final message exactly: `PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>`. Above it, 2-4 lines on what you did.
